alternate_names: Ellora of the North / Ajanta-Ellora of the Himalayas
deities: Saura tradition figures; an unusual idol of Ram, Sita and Lakshman

history.dynasty: Patronage uncertain - popularly attributed to the Katoch dynasty (some sources name Raja Sahil Varman); art-historical analysis (Meister) points to influence of central-Indian king Yasovarman rather than a named local patron
history.period: Early 8th century CE (first half, per Michael Meister); Nagara style
history.summary: TOWN CORRECTION: CSV town 'Kangra' is wrong - the complex stands at Masroor (Masrur) village, about 35 km west of Kangra town. The Masroor temples are North India's finest monolithic rock-cut complex: 15 shrines carved from a single sandstone rock on a square-grid mandala plan, facing northeast toward the Dhauladhar range, with a sacred pool (25x50 m) in front. Dedicated to Shiva, Vishnu, Devi and Saura traditions within a henotheistic framework, it is regarded as the first specimen of a single-rock temple in the Himalayas. Archaeological study suggests the original plan was far more ambitious and the complex was left incomplete. First reported in colonial surveys in 1887, photographed by Henry Shuttleworth in 1913, and surveyed for ASI by Harold Hargreaves in 1915. Damaged but not destroyed by the 1905 Kangra earthquake owing to its monolithic construction. CONFLICTS: popular accounts credit the Katoch dynasty / Raja Sahil Varman or the Pandavas (legend), while scholarly work (Meister) attributes the style to Yasovarman's central-Indian influence with Kashmir-region guild collaboration; the main entrance orientation is reported as northeast (Wikipedia) vs east (some travel sites). Coordinates are from Wikipedia/GeoHack (32.07256, 76.13708), corroborating the general geocoder location. Protected by the Archaeological Survey of India.

name: Masroor Rock Cut Temple
town_description: Masroor (Masrur) is a small village in Kangra district, Himachal Pradesh, about 35 km west of Kangra town in the Beas river valley, known almost entirely for its 8th-century rock-cut temple complex.

travel.airport: Dharamshala (Gaggal) Airport is the nearest airport; the closest major airports with daily services are Amritsar and Jammu (Wikipedia; distances verify).
travel.railway: Nagrota Surian is the nearest railway station (per Wikipedia).
travel.road: About 35 km west of Kangra town and 45 km southwest of Dharamshala-McLeod Ganj; reached via the Lunj-Masroor road through the Kangra valley.

visitor_information.best_time: October to March for clear views of the Dhauladhar range; year-round for the heritage visit.
visitor_information.opening_hours: ASI-protected monument; visit during daylight hours (typically sunrise to sunset). Entry free for casual worship/tourism (verify current ASI rules on site).
